story.title: Rescue Teams Save Woman After 36 Hours Trapped in Colombia Earthquake Rubble
story.summary: A 32-year-old woman was rescued alive after being trapped for 36 hours under the rubble of a collapsed building in Pereira, Colombia, following a 7.4-magnitude earthquake. Rescuers located her 10 hours before successfully reaching her, as they continue to search for more survivors amid the devastation.

explore_lenses.label: Why did the rescue take so long?
explore_lenses.title: Deep debris made extraction hazardous
explore_lenses.summary: The reported 10-hour gap between locating Daniela Largo Sánchez and freeing her reflects the risks of moving through unstable collapsed material, not simply a delay in finding her.

claims.text: Bogotá firefighters said crews located Largo Sánchez about 10 hours before her rescue but could not immediately extract her because she was buried too deeply.
Firefighters said they worked carefully through the debris to reach her without causing another collapse, illustrating the tradeoff between speed and rescuer/survivor safety.
Aid agencies regard the first 48 to 72 hours after a collapse as especially important for finding people alive, although survival can extend beyond that when trapped people have food and water.

Aid agencies regard the first 48 to 72 hours after a collapse as especially important for finding people alive, although survival can extend beyond that when trapped people have food and water.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: Public reporting did not establish Largo Sánchez's medical condition after transport or the precise structural conditions inside the building.

explore_lenses.label: How severe is the wider emergency?
explore_lenses.title: Rescue figures and missing counts are still moving
explore_lenses.summary: The individual rescue occurred within a much larger disaster across western Colombia, but the true number of people missing and the eventual casualty total remained unsettled as of August 12.

claims.text: President Abelardo de la Espriella said by Tuesday that the magnitude 7.4 quake had killed at least 181 people and injured 2,595 in western Colombia.
The president put the number of missing people at at least 195, while civilian-run databases listed nearly 4,000; the gap reflects incomplete information rather than competing confirmed totals.
Deaths and major damage were reported in Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdó, while local leaders and families voiced concern that rural-area impacts were still poorly documented.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the rescue phase?
explore_lenses.title: Aid and recovery operations are expanding
explore_lenses.summary: Authorities are pairing the immediate search with emergency financing and outside assistance, while humanitarian organizations say the earthquake has compounded needs in areas already affected by displacement and armed conflict.

claims.text: The government declared an emergency to speed funding for recovery after initial assessments found roughly 1,600 damaged buildings, including at least 61 that had completely collapsed.
Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council, said the quake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation and requires greater support for the response.

María José Torres, the U.N. resident coordinator in Colombia, said aid organizations already operating in conflict-affected areas, including Chocó near the epicenter, have increased capacity to be present with affected communities.
The United States offered more than $15 million in assistance, while Mexico and El Salvador said they planned to send personnel, supplies or aid shipments.

story_report.summary: A 32-year-old woman was pulled alive from the rubble of a collapsed building 36 hours after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia. Rescue crews had located her about 10 hours earlier but needed time to reach her safely. By Tuesday, President Abelardo de la Espriella said the quake had killed at least 181 people and injured 2,595, leaving emergency teams to contend with widespread destruction and an uncertain number of missing people.

sections.heading: Rescue Crews Navigate Collapse Risks
sections.body: Bogotá firefighters said the woman, identified as Largo Sánchez, was buried too deeply for an immediate extraction after crews found her. Firefighters worked cautiously through the debris to avoid triggering another collapse, balancing the urgency of the rescue against the safety of both the survivor and responders. Aid agencies consider the first 48 to 72 hours after a building collapse especially important for finding survivors, though people can live longer when they have access to food and water.

sections.heading: Earthquake Damage Spans Western Colombia
sections.body: Deaths and major damage were reported in Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdó, while local leaders and families said the effects in rural areas remained poorly documented. The government’s initial assessment found about 1,600 damaged buildings, including at least 61 that had completely collapsed. The president put the number of missing people at at least 195, while civilian-run databases listed nearly 4,000, a gap attributed to incomplete information rather than competing confirmed totals.

sections.heading: Emergency Declaration Speeds Recovery Funding
sections.body: The government declared an emergency to accelerate funding for recovery. Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council, said the quake had compounded an already severe humanitarian situation and required greater support. María José Torres, the U.N. resident coordinator, said organizations working in conflict-affected areas, including Chocó near the epicenter, had expanded their capacity; the United States offered more than $15 million in assistance, while Mexico and El Salvador planned aid shipments, supplies or personnel.

unresolved.text: Largo Sánchez's medical condition after transport and the precise structural conditions inside the collapsed building were not publicly established.

Casualty, injury and missing-person totals remain provisional as teams reach damaged and rural locations; the duration of search operations, foreign-aid delivery timelines and long-term rebuilding needs were also not established.
